summary: This informational document reviews the MPLS protocol suite in the context of IPv6 and identifies gaps that must be addressed before MPLS protocols and applications can run in IPv6-only networks.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7439 checks whether MPLS works on a network that has no IPv4 addresses at all. It looks at each part of the MPLS standards in turn and records whether it can run without IPv4, whether it needs a small clarification, or whether it needs real work. Most of the forwarding and traffic engineering is fine; the label distribution protocol and the diagnostic tools are the problem areas.

questions: can mpls run on ipv6-only networks
subtitle: What in the MPLS suite still assumes IPv4, and what has to change for an IPv6-only network.

tldr.problem: Networks are moving to IPv6-only, but parts of the MPLS protocol suite still assume IPv4, so an operator who rebuilds the core without IPv4 can find that some MPLS features no longer work.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7439 goes through the MPLS standards one at a time, in the data plane, the control plane, the applications and the operations tools, and marks each as having no gap, a major gap or a minor gap, with the work in progress that would close it.
tldr.outcome: The findings are a work list rather than a specification. The data plane, RSVP-TE, path computation and BGP are clear; the label distribution protocol and the operations tools are not, and the document says which drafts are meant to fix them.

today: RFC 7439 is an Informational RFC published in January 2015, and the unit metadata lists no document that obsoletes or updates it. It is a gap analysis and a work list: the drafts it points at were unfinished at the time, and the document says they may be replaced by other solutions.

sections.title: Why MPLS Needs IPv6 Support
sections.content:
IPv6 is an integral part of modern network deployments, but at the time this document was written most deployments were dual-stack, with IPv4 and IPv6 supported equally on many or all nodes, and single-stack mainly meaning IPv4-only devices. Dual stack gives a useful margin for protocols and features that cannot yet operate over IPv6 alone, because they can keep using IPv4 where they need to. As IPv6 deployment becomes more widespread and IPv4 exhaustion begins to change how addresses are consumed, more networks will need some or all of their nodes to operate primarily on IPv6, with a few legacy features on IPv4, or with no IPv4 provisioned on the device at all. That transition exposes any place where a feature, protocol or implementation still needs IPv4 to work properly.

The document follows the recommendation in RFC 6540 that implementations should stop requiring IPv4 for proper and complete function. It reviews the MPLS protocol suite in the context of IPv6 and identifies the gaps that must be addressed so that MPLS protocols and applications can be used on IPv6-only and IPv6-primary networks, the latter being networks where most functions use IPv6 and only a few legacy features use IPv4. Its scope is the standards that define the MPLS suite, not the state of particular vendor implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: Most networks run both address families today, and that is what has allowed MPLS features to keep using IPv4 where they need to. As IPv4 addresses run short and networks are rebuilt without IPv4, anything in MPLS that assumes IPv4 will stop working. The document goes through the MPLS standards looking for those places.

sections.title: The Driver: Networks Full of Managed Devices
sections.content:
The use case that makes this matter is the growth of devices that are managed over IP: set-top boxes for video distribution, the electronics in cell towers, wireless access points, and devices for machine-to-machine and Internet of Things applications. Some of these classes are deployed in the thousands or even millions across a network. The scale of such networks, together with the increasingly overlapping use of private IPv4 address space inside the average network and the lack of globally routable IPv4 space for long-term growth, drives the need for many endpoints to be managed solely over IPv6. Even where those devices carry IPv4 user data, it is often encapsulated in another protocol, so the link between the endpoint and its upstream devices can be IPv6-only without affecting IPv4 support for the user data. As the number of devices to manage grows, the operator has to move to IPv6, and depending on the MPLS features required, the existing MPLS network will have to be extended to reach those devices.

As the effect of IPv4 exhaustion becomes more acute, more aggressive reclamation of IPv4 addresses becomes justified. Networks are likely to reserve their remaining IPv4 addresses for revenue-generating customers so that legacy support can last as long as necessary, which means the infrastructure itself, including the label switching and label edge routers, may have its IPv4 addresses reclaimed and move to IPv6-only operation.

The baseline for the analysis is that some endpoints and some provider edge and provider routers have only IPv6 transport and must support the full set of MPLS features at parity with an IPv4 network, whether the labels are distributed by LDP, RSVP-TE or BGP, and whether they are carried in MPLS, IP, GRE or L2TPv3. The document separates user data from control plane data, since some of the payload carried on an IPv6-only MPLS network may still be IPv4. Gaps are called major when a standard needs significant change because it lacks the functionality for IPv6-only operation or explicitly requires IPv4 with no IPv6 alternative, and minor when the change is mainly a clarification of wording that leaves IPv6 support implicit or omitted but unlikely to stop IPv6-only operation.
sections.plainLanguage: The pressure comes from the number of devices a network has to manage: television boxes, base stations, wireless access points and small sensors, often in the millions, with no spare IPv4 addresses left. Those devices can be managed over IPv6 even while carrying IPv4 traffic of their own, so the network that manages them has to speak IPv6, and if that network is an MPLS one, the MPLS side has to cope.

sections.title: The Gaps in the Data Plane and the Control Plane
sections.content:
The data plane has no gap: labelled packets travel over many kinds of data link, and the encapsulations of MPLS in IP and GRE and MPLS over L2TPv3 all support IPv6.

In the control plane, the Label Distribution Protocol was designed for an IPv4 or dual-stack network and has deficiencies that stop it working in an IPv6-only one, covering the mapping of paths to labels, the protocol's own identifiers, neighbour discovery, session establishment, the next-hop address and the time-to-live security mechanism. The gap is major, and an update to the protocol was in progress that was expected to close it.

Multipoint LDP inherits the LDP control plane gaps, because it uses LDP to find its peers and set up sessions. It has an area of its own: it defines its own forwarding equivalence classes, and each contains a root address that is an IP address, which the current specification allows to be chosen by address family, so IPv6 root addresses need no extension. The root address is used by each router on the path to find the upstream neighbour towards the root, which is a problem when a path crosses both IPv4-only and IPv6-only nodes. The example given has an IPv4-only leaf, a dual-stack router, an IPv6-only router, another IPv6-only router, a dual-stack router and an IPv4-only root: with the leaf using the root's IPv4 address, the setup fails at the first IPv6-only router, because it cannot look up reachability to an IPv4 address. A solution defined for a backbone with no route to the root could be extended to the same purpose, with a border router translating the root address between address families. The gap is major.

Everything else in the control plane has no gap. RSVP-TE can set up a path for an IPv4 or IPv6 prefix. The traffic engineering extensions to OSPF version 3 and IS-IS exist for IPv6. The point-to-multipoint extensions of RSVP-TE support both address families, and so does fast reroute, including the loop-free alternates used for local protection. The path computation element communication protocol is defined for both address families, with discovery through the interior gateway protocol using IPv4 or IPv6 addresses, and the extensions for confidentiality, route exclusions, monitoring and point-to-multipoint paths all support both. BGP can distribute a label for an IPv4 or IPv6 prefix in an IPv6-only network. Generalized MPLS has one minor gap: a mapping in the transport profile identifier specification assumes that node identifiers are derived from valid IPv4 addresses, an assumption that fails when there are no IPv4 addresses at all.
sections.plainLanguage: Carrying labelled packets is fine, because the encapsulations already work over IPv6. Most of the signalling is fine too: the traffic engineering extensions, the path computation protocol and BGP all handle IPv6. The exception is the label distribution protocol, which was written for IPv4 and needs six separate fixes, plus the multipoint version of it, which inherits those fixes and has an extra problem when a path crosses a mixed network.

sections.title: The Gaps in the Applications and in Operations
sections.content:
For Layer 2 VPNs, very few changes are needed: the signalling runs over BGP or LDP, and both work over IPv6. One document has a minor gap, because it suggests encoding the provider edge address in the instance identifier, which is limited to 12 bytes so that it can be told apart from another encoding, and because it suggests encoding the address in identifiers that are limited to 32 bits. Ethernet VPN uses the functions of LDP and multipoint LDP, so it inherits the LDP gaps and, once those are resolved, should work on IPv6-only networks.

For Layer 3 VPNs there are two use cases: connecting IPv6 islands over an IPv6-only MPLS network, and connecting IPv4 islands over one. Both require mapping IP packets onto an IPv6-signalled path. The base specification defines IPv4 VPNs with 32-bit next-hop addresses, and a later document adds IPv6 support with 128-bit next-hop addresses, but that document does not formally update the base one, so an implementer may miss it, and it explicitly puts the second use case out of scope. That use case, where IPv4 edge devices must map IPv4 traffic onto paths signalled over IPv6 and the core switches may not understand IPv4 at all, is not specified in any RFC. The gap is major, and the related extension documents need an update to cover it explicitly.

For multicast VPNs and for the transport profile, the gaps are the ones already identified or none at all. The transport profile does not require IP, so it is out of scope and unaffected.

The operations tools are where the serious gaps are. Most of the mechanisms work in pure IPv6, but mixed environments cause problems. Extended ICMP works for IPv4 and IPv6, yet the mechanisms may fail when tunnelling IPv4 traffic over a path carried by IPv6-only infrastructure: if the IPv4 time-to-live expires at a router inside the path, that router should examine the IPv4 payload and send an ICMPv4 message, but it is not IPv4-aware and cannot do either, so no message reaches the source. The document notes that this is a general problem with tunnelling when address families do not match, not something specific to MPLS, and so will be hard to fix in MPLS alone. LSP Ping has three problems. It is specified to work with IPv6, but the target address for IPv6 is a randomly chosen address from the range 0:0:0:0:0:FFFF:127/104, which is an IPv4-mapped IPv6 address, and the document says this transitional mechanism should not bleed into IPv6-only networks. The mechanism needs a range of loopback addresses to exercise equal-cost multipath, but the IPv6 address architecture gives only one loopback address, and no value is defined for the IPv6 router alert option, where IPv4 uses zero. Finally, the way a 32-bit router identifier is carried in a 128-bit field is not described. The gap is major. The other operations mechanisms are clear: bidirectional forwarding detection is specified for IPv4 and IPv6 versions of the forwarding equivalence classes and runs over UDP on both, pseudowire operations are defined for both address families, and the transport profile operations do not require IP.

For management information modules, the textual conventions for MPLS lack IPv6 support in two of their definitions, and work was under way to mark them obsolete. The other module specifications for the router, the label distribution protocol and traffic engineering already support both address families. The gap is minor.
sections.plainLanguage: The applications have two real problems. Connecting IPv4 customers over a core that only speaks IPv6 is not specified anywhere, and the documents that come closest leave it out of scope. The diagnostic tools are worse: when an IPv4 packet expires inside an IPv6-only path, the router cannot build the error message, so the sender never learns. The path ping tool also relies on IPv4-shaped addresses, and on a value for the IPv6 router alert option that nobody has defined.

sections.title: The Gap Summary
sections.content:
The document closes with a table of the gaps it found and the work in progress that would address them. The label distribution protocol has gaps in path mapping, identifiers, discovery, session establishment, the next-hop address and time-to-live security, addressed by the IPv6 update to that protocol. Multipoint LDP inherits those gaps and the ones in the document about multipoint trees in a backbone with no route to the root, and may need extra fixes to that document. Generalized MPLS has the node identifier derivation gap, with nothing yet decided. The Layer 2 VPN gap in discovery and signalling has no fix yet. The Layer 3 VPN gap, that the later document does not define a method for the two mixed cases, has no fix yet. The operations gap, that the path ping specification has no IPv6 multipath support and no IPv6 router alert value and may drop messages when the versions do not match, is addressed by work on the router alert value. The management module gap is addressed by the work on the textual conventions.

The document is careful about what this table means. The documents it points at are works in progress without consensus, so other solutions may be proposed later, and the pointers should not be considered normative in any way. Work in progress on new features that use MPLS protocols will have to make sure those protocols work on IPv6-only or IPv6-primary networks, or say explicitly which of the gaps they depend on.
sections.plainLanguage: The summary table lists the six areas with gaps and where the fix is supposed to come from. Two of them, the label distribution protocol and the operations tools, have work in progress behind them. The others had nothing decided at the time. The document is careful to say that the drafts it names were not agreed, so they may be replaced by something else.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Changing the address family used to operate the MPLS network does not fundamentally alter the security considerations that apply to any of the specifics of the protocol or its features. The follow-on work recommended by the gap analysis does, however, have to consider any effect that the use of IPv6 in the modifications may have on security.
sections.plainLanguage: Moving the network to IPv6 does not change the security story of MPLS itself, since the same rules apply whatever addresses are used. The patches that fix the gaps do have to think about whether using IPv6 in them opens anything new.
